brief.topic: Why a handful of passing demo prompts is not an evaluation, and what to build instead
brief.audience: PMs moving into AI product management and product leaders shipping GenAI features
constraints: No employer, customer or vendor references
Illustrative numbers must be labelled on screen
Text-on-screen reel: no TTS provider configured in this environment

coreInsight: Prompts your team picked because they work only test the happy path; ship against an eval set of real inputs with expected behaviour and a consistent pass rule.

hooks.text: Five great demo prompts are not an evaluation.
hooks.notes: Names the exact practice most teams follow; understandable in under two seconds; makes no claim the reel can't back up.

hooks.text: Your AI feature passed the demo. That proves almost nothing.
hooks.notes: Strong curiosity, but 'almost nothing' overstates the case and reads as hype.

hooks.text: Before you ship an AI feature, build this one test set.
hooks.notes: Useful, but 'this one test set' is vague until later in the reel; weaker first two seconds.

selectionRationale: Highest total (24/25). It names a concrete, widespread mistake, is fully understood from the first frame, and the reel delivers exactly what it promises: why the demo misleads and what to use instead.

scenes.purpose: Deliver the better approach concretely: what an eval case contains, using the same inputs the viewer just saw.

scenes.purpose: Make the consequence tangible with a clearly labelled illustrative comparison, then turn it into a positive reframe.

scenes.voiceover: In this illustrative example, the same feature scores five out of five on the demo, and thirty-one out of fifty on real cases. That gap is your actual roadmap.

caption.opening: Five demo prompts that all pass tell you one thing: your team knows which prompts work.
body:
They don't tell you how the feature handles:
→ vague, typo-filled questions
→ questions with missing context
→ requests it should refuse or hand off
→ long, messy documents
→ users trying to get around the rules

Before launch, build an eval set: real inputs from logs and support tickets, the behaviour you expect for each one, and a pass rule you apply the same way every time. Rerun it whenever the prompt, model or retrieval changes.
The gap between your demo score and your eval score isn't bad news. It's your real roadmap.
(The 5/5 vs 31/50 in the reel is an illustrative example, not data from a real product.)

claims.text: Prompts chosen by the team because they work over-represent the happy path and don't reflect real user inputs.
An eval set pairs real inputs with expected behaviour and a consistent pass rule, and should be rerun when the prompt, model or retrieval changes.

publish.notes: Evergreen; no time-sensitive claims. Post when your audience is most active (check Instagram Insights once you have a baseline).

carousel: 1/ Five great demo prompts are not an evaluation.
2/ Why the demo misleads: the team wrote the prompts and kept the ones that worked.
3/ What real users send: typos, missing context, out-of-scope asks, messy files, rule-breaking attempts.
4/ Anatomy of an eval case: INPUT → EXPECTED BEHAVIOUR → PASS RULE (with the three examples).
5/ Where to get inputs: logs, support tickets, SME-written edge cases, past escalations.
6/ When to rerun: every prompt, model, or retrieval change; track pass rate over time.
7/ Save-able summary card + 'Save this for your next launch review'.
repurposing.followUpReel: Format 2 (Framework): 'How to write a pass rule for an AI answer' — exact match vs rubric vs human review, and when each is worth the cost.
repurposing.linkedin: Text post opening with the demo-vs-eval gap as a PM lesson; 3 short paragraphs on where eval inputs come from and how to make pass rules consistent; ask peers how they source edge cases. No numbers presented as real data.
